analysis.one_liner: Extends enhanced ACA health insurance premium tax credits through 2027 and tightens broker fraud and Medicare Advantage payment rules.
analysis.headline: Backed by 12 cosponsors including 7 Republicans, the bill has sat in two House committees with no markup or vote since its November 10, 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits, which lower the cost of insurance bought through the marketplaces, are scheduled to lapse after 2025. This bill extends them through 2027, raises the income cutoff from 400% to 600% of the poverty line, and lowers the share of income enrollees must pay toward premiums. It also cracks down on insurance brokers who enroll or switch people into plans without their consent, and tightens Medicare Advantage payment rules to reduce payments based on inflated patient-risk coding.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy health insurance on the ACA marketplaces—especially middle- and upper-middle-income households above 400% of the poverty line, who lose eligibility when the enhanced credits lapse—would keep help through 2027. Marketplace enrollees also gain broker-fraud protections, and taxpayers gain from tighter Medicare Advantage payment rules.

how_it_helps.text: For 2026 and 2027, the bill keeps premiums at 0% of income for households up to 150% of the poverty line and lowers the required premium percentage at every income tier, with a top rate of 8.5%.
It raises the income cap for receiving the credit from 400% to 600% of the poverty line for taxable years in 2026 and 2027.

It creates civil penalties of $10,000 to $50,000 per affected applicant for negligent misinformation by agents or brokers, up to $200,000 per person for knowing fraud, and criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison for knowing and willful fraud.

It requires broker-assisted enrollments to include documented consent, delays broker commissions until data inconsistencies are resolved, notifies enrollees of changes with instructions for canceling unauthorized activity, and bars disenrolling people without their consent.

It tightens Medicare Advantage risk adjustment by requiring two years of diagnostic data, excluding diagnoses gathered from chart reviews and health risk assessments, and requiring an annual public evaluation of coding-pattern differences between plans and providers.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the extended credits; the bill contains no offsetting revenue. Medicare Advantage insurers would receive less through risk-adjusted payments, and insurance agents, brokers, and marketing firms would bear penalties and new compliance requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; Medicare Advantage insurers and brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill extends the credits with no pay-for; it contains no revenue provisions or offsets for the added federal cost.
The extension lasts only through 2027, so enrollees face the same expiration cliff again at the end of 2027.

Agents and brokers could argue the new per-person penalties, consent documentation, and commission-delay rules push liability onto small brokers and could reduce the number of agents willing to help consumers enroll.

Medicare Advantage plans could argue that excluding chart-review diagnoses and adding coding-intensity adjustments cuts payments for plans that accurately document sicker patients, potentially pressuring benefits or provider networks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill—keeping marketplace coverage affordable through 2027—delivers large, concrete help to enrollees, and the anti-fraud provisions address real enrollment abuses while explicitly protecting victims from losing coverage. The honest costs are forgone federal revenue with no offsets, a two-year design that sets up another expiration fight in 2027, and reduced Medicare Advantage payments that plans will contest. On balance the benefits to enrollees and taxpayers outweigh those costs, but the temporary structure limits the good it does.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced November 10, 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees; neither has scheduled a markup or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 10, 2025 by Rep. Sam Liccardo with Reps. Kiley, Bacon, Goodlander, and Ross as original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It has 12 cosponsors, 7 Republicans and 5 Democrats.
The action history shows no further activity after the initial referral—no markup, hearing, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost on the merits; the bill has simply not moved, leaving the subsidy extension unresolved while marketplace plans and enrollees face uncertainty about premiums for 2026.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet—bill untouched in committee

sides.party_line_note: The 12 cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 7 Republicans; no votes have occurred, so the record shows only bipartisan sponsorship so far.

industries.note: The extension keeps federal premium subsidies flowing through marketplace plans for two more years, locking in the insurers' subsidized customer base even as the broker-fraud rules police enrollment practices. The insurers' interest in continued subsidies runs alongside enrollees' interest in affordable premiums.

The bill imposes per-person civil penalties up to $200,000, up to 10 years' imprisonment for knowing fraud, consent documentation, commission delays until inconsistencies are resolved, and audits of broker conduct. Agents who enrolled or switched consumers without consent profited at enrollees' expense.

Risk adjustment changes—two years of diagnostic data, exclusion of chart-review and health-risk-assessment diagnoses, and a coding-intensity adjustment—would reduce payments tied to documenting sicker patients. Excess coding has been paid for by taxpayers.

They must register with the Secretary, meet conduct and marketing criteria, forgo unapproved referral compensation, and report agent terminations. Their lead-generation and enrollment-switching business model comes under direct federal criteria for the first time in the ACA marketplace.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce with no scheduled action. Extension of the enhanced premium credits is being negotiated at a higher level after their scheduled end-of-2025 expiration, and standalone extensions like this one typically advance only if attached to a larger package that House leadership agrees to bring up. With narrow margins and leadership controlling the calendar, a standalone floor vote on this bill is unlikely in the near term.
